short: Name's Abner Keller. I farm wheat outside Lancaster, and I'm no hand at speeches, so I'll keep this short.
You ever watch a loaded wagon on a dirt road in April? It sinks. Every hour it sits in the mud, some farmer loses money.

So here's the plan. Sixty-two miles from Philadelphia to Lancaster. Broken stone and gravel on a graded bed, with a stone bridge over the Brandywine. Built the way they build roads in Europe. Not dirt. Stone.
Who pays? The people who use it. Nine toll gates. A traveler pays, the spiked pole gets turned aside, and the money comes to you.
We're selling one thousand shares at three hundred dollars each. The law caps our dividend at fifteen percent, so don't go dreaming.

Now I'll be straight with you. Roads cost more than anyone says. If we run short, we sell more shares. And when the sign-up opened, there was such an uproar that shares had to be handed out by lottery. I don't trust anything folks fight over.
But a farmer pays that toll every time, in rain or snow. It won't make you rich by Christmas. It'll pay you year after year.
If you want something dull and dependable, put your name down. If you want excitement, there's a fellow down the hall.
Come closer. Closer. I shouldn't say this in a room this size.
England makes the best cotton thread in the world, and England means to keep it that way. Their law forbids anyone to carry the plans for those spinning machines out of the country.

So a young man named Samuel Slater, twenty-one, apprenticed in an English mill, carried no plans. Nothing to find in a trunk. He memorized them. Every gear, every roller, every spindle. Then he crossed the ocean in 1789, dressed as a farmhand.

Now he's in Pawtucket, Rhode Island. Mr. Moses Brown's firm had bought a machine nobody could run, and Slater called it worthless. So he built new ones from memory. By December of 1790, he had a carding machine and seventy-two spindles running.

Now we're building a proper mill beside the falls on the Blackstone River. The river turns a wheel, and the wheel drives every machine. Water doesn't rest. Water doesn't ask for a raise. Machines like these can do the work of hundreds of hand spinners.
Who tends the machines? Children. Small hands, small wages.
No one else in America can do this. No one. If you want in, tell nobody where you heard it.

Step right up, step right up! Have you heard about the boat that needs no wind? No oars? No mules? Everybody laughed. They called it Fulton's Folly. Then last August it went a hundred and fifty miles up the Hudson River to Albany at five miles an hour, and nobody's laughing now!
A fire under a boiler makes steam, steam turns the paddle wheels, and steam doesn't read the weather report!
Sailing sloops wait for the wind. Our boat runs on a schedule, and you can sell tickets to a schedule. Passengers, freight, mail, all on time.

Now here's the beautiful part. The State of New York has given Mr. Livingston and Mr. Fulton the exclusive right to run steamboats on every river and lake in the state. Thirty more years! If any other steamboat shows up without our permission, the state seizes it. Seizes it, friends! No competitors. None!
So when you buy a share, you're not buying one boat. You're buying the whole river.
Returns? Enormous. Fabulous. I don't have the numbers on me, but a gentleman in Albany is already ordering a second boat, and he is very, very happy.
But hurry! Shares like this don't last. Who's in? Who's in? Right here, sir, I see that hand!
Gentlemen! Ladies! Look at this map, and let me show you the future.

Here is the Hudson River, carrying the wealth of New York to the sea. And here, three hundred and sixty-three miles to the west, is Lake Erie, and behind it an entire continent of wheat, timber, and farmland with no road to market. Between them, nothing but mud, hills, and a wagon that charges one hundred dollars to haul a single ton.
I propose to close that gap with water.

A canal from Albany to Buffalo, with eighty-three locks to lift boats over five hundred and sixty-eight feet of land. And the price of shipping a ton? Not one hundred dollars. Ten. Ten dollars, gentlemen!
The cost is estimated at seven million dollars, and the State of New York will build it. Tolls from every boat will flow into a Canal Fund, and that fund will repay you.
Yes, my rivals call it Clinton's Folly. Let them! No American has ever dug anything like it. And winter? Winter is only a brief rest for the mules. Spring returns, and so will the boats.
Seven million dollars buys us the Great Lakes. Invest now, and you will stand on the bank when the first boat passes.
Friends! Neighbors! Sit down, sit down. I've got the greatest opportunity in the history of Illinois, and I'm letting you in before the crowds arrive.

You've seen the wagons in the mud. You've seen the rivers freeze in December and shrink in August. Well, we are done with rivers, because our great state has passed the Internal Improvement Act. Thirteen hundred miles of railroad. Ten million dollars of vision. And the very first line, the Northern Cross, runs from Quincy through Springfield to the Indiana line.
A steam locomotive, brand new from New Jersey, is on its way. Three trains a week! Three!
And it's cheap. We're not wasting money on fancy iron rails. We lay wood, with a thin iron strap on top. Same train, half the price. Smart, isn't it?
A gentleman in Springfield bought Illinois bonds early, and he can't stop smiling. Wouldn't tell me his name. Modest fellow.
And don't listen to the doomsayers about banks failing back East. That's New York's trouble, not ours. Nobody who bought Illinois bonds ever regretted it. Nobody.
But I have room for only three more investors. The state wants its money by the end of the week, and if you wait, the price will go up. Guaranteed.
So who wants to say, I was there at the beginning?
